prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: They, The, Mother

outputs.L1:
They grow in number all the time:  
the cat, the mother, the father,  
the grandparents, aunts, and uncles—  
those I knew well and those I hardly knew at all;  
my best friend from when I was ten;  
the guy who sat with me in the back  
of the class, where the tall kids lived;  
Bill the Shoemaker from Lyndale Avenue;  
the Irish poet with rounded handwriting.

They live in the Land of Echo,  
the Land of Reverb, and I hear them between  
the notes of the birds, the plash of the wave  
on the smooth rocks. They show up  
when I think of them, as if they are always  
waiting for me to remember.

I drive by their empty houses.  
I put on their old sweaters and caps.  
I wear their wristwatches and spend  
their money. So now I’m in six places  
at once—if not eighteen or twenty—  
so many places to be thinking of them.

Strange how quiet they are in their presence,  
so humble in the low song they sing,  
not expecting that anyone will listen.
outputs.L2:
Their ranks keep increasing:  
the cat; my mother and father;  
grandparents, aunts, and uncles—  
some close to me, others nearly strangers;  
the friend I loved most at ten;  
the boy beside me in the classroom’s rear,  
the territory reserved for taller children;  
Bill, the cobbler on Lyndale Avenue;  
and the poet from Ireland whose script curved softly.

They inhabit the Country of Echoes,  
the Realm of Reverberation.  
I catch their voices in the spaces  
between birdsong and the splash of water  
against stones worn smooth.

The moment they enter my thoughts, they appear,  
as though they have been standing by,  
waiting to be recalled.  
I pass the homes they left vacant,  
pull on their aging sweaters and hats,  
fasten their watches around my wrist,  
and use the money that once belonged to them.

Because of this, I occupy six places simultaneously—  
perhaps eighteen, perhaps twenty—  
all the many locations where memory finds them.

How quietly they make themselves known,  
how modestly their low melody continues,  
asking for no listener at all.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s memories hold an ever-growing community of the dead: relatives, friends, acquaintances, and admired figures who have shaped their life in different ways. These people now inhabit a metaphorical “Land of Echo,” where their presence lingers in natural sounds, familiar surroundings, and moments of silence. Whenever the speaker remembers them, they seem to return, as though they have been patiently waiting to be called back into consciousness.

This connection is sustained through the objects and spaces they left behind—empty houses, old clothes, wristwatches, money, and other personal belongings. Such ordinary things become vessels of memory, preserving traces of the people who once used or inhabited them. Through these recollections, the speaker is carried across many times and places at once. The dead remain present in a quiet and humble way, neither demanding recognition nor asking for attention, but simply accompanying the speaker through the continuing echoes of their lives.
outputs.L4:
Grief has taught the speaker that the dead do not simply disappear. As the years pass, their presence seems to grow, returning through the ordinary details of daily life. A familiar room can suddenly hold the memory of someone once loved; an old coat, a photograph, or a small object kept in a drawer can bring back the warmth of a hand or the shape of a smile. Certain roads, houses, and landscapes remain inhabited by those who once walked there, so that revisiting them feels like entering the past and the present at the same time.

The departed also make themselves known through sound. Their voices seem to linger in the rustling of leaves, the call of a bird, the movement of water, or the wind passing softly through the trees. These are not loud or frightening visitations, but quiet echoes that accompany the speaker in unexpected moments. Memory allows the dead to exist beside the living—not as they once did, but in a gentler and more enduring form.

In this way, remembrance becomes a kind of shared life. The people who have been lost continue to appear in places, possessions, sensations, and natural sounds, humbly woven into the speaker’s world. Grief does not restore them, yet neither does it permit them to vanish completely. Through love and memory, they remain present across time, quietly accompanying the speaker and continuing to shape the life that goes on without them.
outputs.L5: They gathered beneath the old oak at dawn, speaking in whispers as the sky slowly brightened. The village had changed, but the Mother remained—patient, watchful, and strong. She welcomed them home without questions, opening her arms as though no time had passed. In that quiet embrace, they remembered who they were and where they belonged.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem about remembering deceased family members, childhood friends, and forgotten acquaintances who continue to live quietly through memories and inherited belongings.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the House Remembers**

In the back of the cupboard  
my grandmother’s blue bowl  
holds nothing now  
but a pale ring of dust.

Still, when I lift it,  
her hands rise beneath mine—  
flour at the knuckles,  
a small gold band  
worn thin by years of washing.

My father survives  
in the stubborn watch  
that loses four minutes every day,  
in the coat whose pockets  
keep yielding screws, receipts,  
a peppermint gone soft with age.

There are others.

A childhood friend  
runs forever through sprinklers  
at the edge of an August lawn,  
calling my name  
as if evening will never arrive.

The boy from two streets over  
leans his bicycle against the sky.  
A teacher bends above my desk,  
smelling of chalk and rain.  
A woman whose name I have forgotten  
once gave me an orange  
at a winter bus stop.

Even she remains—  
not whole, not gone—  
but bright as the peel  
opening in my hands.

We carry the dead  
without knowing their weight:

in a recipe written sideways,  
in the habit of saving string,  
in a laugh that startles us  
because it belongs to an uncle,  
in the way we fold a towel  
exactly as someone taught us  
and never said goodbye.

At night, the house settles  
around these quiet inheritances—  
the clock, the bowl,  
the photographs curling at the corners,  
the names we can still pronounce  
and those worn smooth by forgetting.

Nothing speaks.

Yet everywhere  
a life has left its door ajar,

and memory,  
barefoot and uninvited,  
moves from room to room,  
touching what remains,  
keeping the smallest lamps lit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a reflective poem in the voice of an aging person who senses the dead everywhere—in birdsong, waves, empty houses, old clothes, watches, and money.
counterfactuals.output:
**What Remains Near**

Now that my years have thinned the world,  
the dead come easily.

They borrow the throats of birds at dawn—  
one clear note from the cedar  
and my mother is calling me home,  
though the house she meant  
has long since lost its roof.

Along the shore, each folding wave  
brings back a voice, then takes it.  
I stand ankle-deep among farewells,  
hearing old friends in the foam  
laugh as they did before time  
taught us to count.

Empty houses are never empty.  
Dust keeps the shape of footsteps;  
doors remember hands.  
In an upstairs room, a curtain lifts  
though no window is open,  
and someone almost enters.

I find them in old clothes—  
a shoulder lingering in a coat,  
the faint warmth of a dress  
creased in a cedar chest.  
Even buttons seem faithful,  
holding fast to what they cannot save.

Their watches sleep in drawers,  
small moons with stopped hearts.  
I wind one and listen:  
the dead resume their patient walking,  
second by second, nowhere  
and everywhere at once.

And money—worn coins, soft bills—  
passes through palms like inheritance:  
bread bought, wages paid,  
a child’s fever, a burial.  
How many vanished fingers  
have polished this silver thin?

I used to think death was a country  
beyond the last hill.  
Now I know it is the weather  
moving through all things—

in birdsong, salt, and vacant rooms,  
in cloth, in clocks, in currency—  
a presence neither cruel nor kind,  
only near.

And I, growing quiet,  
begin to hear my own name  
among its many names,  
not as a summons,  
but as a note already trembling  
inside the song.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a lyrical elegy titled “The Land of Echo” about how the number of people we mourn grows over time.
counterfactuals.output:
# The Land of Echo

At first, grief was a single bell  
trembling beyond the hill,  
one name the evening carried  
when every road was still.

Then years went on like rivers,  
taking the light they knew;  
the bell became a chorus,  
the one name widened to two.

Now every field remembers,  
each doorway keeps a tone;  
the wind repeats our lost ones  
in voices not its own.

We walk the land of echo  
where absent footsteps meet,  
where those we mourn grow countless  
as leaves along the street.

And still the heart makes chambers,  
though sorrow crowds the air—  
room after room of silence,  
each silence holding prayer.

Someday our names may mingle  
with rain, with root, with stone;  
and those who follow after  
will think they walk alone—

until at dusk they hear us,  
soft as the grasses blow:  
love never leaves completely.  
It enters echo.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary poem with plainspoken imagery about carrying lost loved ones with you and feeling as though you inhabit many places at once.
counterfactuals.output:
I keep them in ordinary places—

my father in the way I check the locks,  
my aunt in the blue cup by the sink,  
my friend in every song  
I almost turn off.

They do not follow like ghosts.  
They are quieter than that.

They ride in the passenger seat  
while I drive home in the rain.  
They stand beside me at the grocery store  
when I reach for the pears.  
Sometimes one of them laughs  
using my mouth.

I live here, in this apartment  
with its thin walls and one good window,  
but also in the house with the red steps,  
the town where summer smelled like dust,  
the hospital hallway at three in the morning,  
the kitchen where everyone was still alive.

All day I cross these rooms  
without moving.

A train passes.  
The glass trembles.  
For a moment I am twenty, then ten,  
then exactly my age.

I used to think losing someone  
meant they went somewhere  
I could not go.

Now I think the body is a kind of country.  
People leave,  
but not completely.

I carry their weather.  
Their unfinished sentences.  
The small maps of their hands.

Wherever I stand,  
the ground is crowded—

this street, that shore,  
the old backyard under snow.

I am never in one place.

I am never there alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce an intimate, melancholy poem that lists departed people from the speaker’s past, then portrays them as humble presences waiting silently to be remembered.
counterfactuals.output:
My mother, folding dusk into the curtains.  
My brother, whistling through a broken tooth.  
Old Mara from the corner shop,  
who saved bruised pears for me.  
Mr. Vale, the teacher with chalk on his sleeves.  
Eli, who left his red scarf  
on the back of my chair.  
And Anna—  
whose name still opens like a door  
onto a room I cannot enter.

They do not haunt me.

They gather quietly  
in the plainest places:  
the cup cooling beside the sink,  
the stair that sighs beneath my foot,  
the garden after rain.

No halos, no white garments—  
only their patient, familiar faces,  
their hands resting in their laps  
as if they have come early  
and do not wish to trouble me.

They wait without accusation,  
small as dust in afternoon light,  
humble as coats upon their hooks,

until I speak a name  
and one of them looks up.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
